listenings.text: The thing people get wrong about agricultural credit is that they compare it to a mortgage, and it is nothing like a mortgage. A mortgage is a person with a salary that arrives on the same day every month. A farm has one payday a year, and it depends on the weather, on a price nobody controls, and on a truck arriving when it should. So the whole question changes. I am not asking whether this customer can pay me in March. I am asking whether this customer will still be standing in March. I have worked in this sector for nineteen years, and the single best predictor I have found is not the balance sheet. It is whether the grower calls me before the problem arrives or after. The ones who call early have almost never defaulted on me. The ones who go quiet in a bad season are the ones I lose sleep over.

I have run this dealership since two thousand and six, and I sit exactly in the middle, which is a strange place to sit. The factory wants its money on the agreed date. The grower wants the product now and the invoice after the harvest, which is seven months later. So I carry the difference, and that is really what a dealer is: a warehouse with a bank attached to it. People assume the hard part is selling. It is not. The hard part is the phone call in a bad year, when a customer I have known for two decades tells me he cannot pay this season. What I have learned is to make that call boring. If we have already agreed what happens in a bad year, before the bad year, nobody has to be brave on the telephone. Almost everything that goes wrong in this business goes wrong because two people avoided one uncomfortable conversation in October.

paras: Somebody who has spent a career in consumer credit and then moves into agribusiness usually says the same thing in the first month: none of the instincts transfer. In consumer credit the customer is paid on the same day every month, and the only real question is how much of that salary is already promised to somebody else. A farm has one payday a year. It arrives after the harvest, and it depends on the weather, on a commodity price that nobody in the room controls, and on a truck turning up when it was supposed to. So the calendar stops being a source of information. An account that looks healthy in October and overdue in April may have exactly the same customer behind it.

This is why the paperwork in the sector looks strange from outside. Payment terms follow the season rather than the month, which means a company is often carrying its receivables for two hundred days without anybody being late. The credit limit is not really a limit on one purchase; it is a decision about how much of one season a company is prepared to finance. And the dealer in the middle is the piece most outsiders miss. A dealer buys from the factory on the factory's terms and sells to the grower on the grower's terms, and lives on the difference between the two dates. That is why four overdue dealers can matter more than eleven overdue farms.

Analysts who have worked in this sector for a long time tend to agree on two things, and neither of them is about numbers. The first is that the customer who telephones before the problem arrives is a different kind of risk from the customer who goes quiet, and that the difference shows up long before it shows up in the accounts. The second is that almost every disaster in agricultural credit began with one uncomfortable conversation that two people avoided in October. Compliance exists for exactly that reason: it is not paperwork, it is what allows an analyst to say no in March and still have the customer in September.
